bridge.The family, and the farm: Now that you know what kind of year this is, let's go and meet the people who live in that white farmhouse. Shall we knock on the door?
bridge.The small town, and the bank holiday: The chores are done, and it's Saturday. Climb into the back of the old car with the children, and let's drive into town.
bridge.The radio, and living on very little: Back home, the evening light is fading. Can you hear that crackle from the parlour? Someone has switched on the radio.
bridge.Drifters, and the farm auction: Not everyone in 1933 had a farm, or a radio, or even a home. Some people were always on the road. Let's sit on the porch and watch them pass.
bridge.The country school, and the neighbours: The road outside is quiet again. Tomorrow is a school day, so you'll want to be up early with June and Eddie.
bridge.The New Deal: Far away from the little schoolhouse, in Washington, big plans were being made. What do you think they meant for a farm family like the Millers?
bridge.Summer, and the world's fair: The new programmes take time to reach the farm. Meanwhile, the summer arrives, hot and bright. Can you feel the sun on your arms?
bridge.The county fair, and the harvest: The big city lights are far behind you now. Back in Iowa, the end of summer brings the best day of the year for a farm boy.
bridge.Thanksgiving, and winter: The corn is in, and the cribs are full. The days grow short and cold. And soon, you'll smell turkey drifting from the kitchen.
bridge.What came later, and what they learned: Let's step out of 1933 for a little while, you and I, and look ahead. What became of the Millers, and of the country around them?
bridge.Iowa today: The years roll on, and the old farm changes. So what would you find if you drove down that same gravel road today?

voor.In 1933, the middle of America: Picture yourself standing at the edge of a cornfield, with the wind in your hair.
voor.For the farmers, it is a very hard time: If you'd been a farmer then, you'd have watched every penny.
voor.In this story, we will follow: You'll get to know them well, I think.
voor.To understand the Great Depression: You might think the trouble began on a farm. It didn't.
voor.Then, in October 1929: You'd have seen worried faces on every street corner.
voor.Then the banks began to fail: You'd walk to your bank and find the doors locked.
voor.Walt Miller is forty-two: If you shook his hand, you'd feel how rough it was from years of work.
voor.Ruth Miller is thirty-nine: You'd find her in the kitchen, almost always, with her sleeves rolled up.
voor.Eddie is nine: You'd hear him long before you saw him.
voor.On the farm, the day begins: You'd wake to a cold, dark room and the sound of the rooster.
voor.In the barn, the animals: You'd smell hay and warm animals as soon as you opened the door.
voor.Meanwhile, in the kitchen: You'd smell bacon and coffee drifting up the stairs.
voor.On Saturday afternoon, the Millers: You'd squeeze into the back seat, between the egg baskets.
voor.On Saturday, the town is busy: You'd see wagons and old cars parked side by side along the street.
voor.The children love Saturdays: You'd feel a penny burning a hole in your pocket.
voor.On the fourth of March, 1933: You'd gather around the radio with your neighbours to listen.
voor.Millions of people listened: You'd lean closer to the speaker so you didn't miss a word.
voor.The most precious thing in the Millers': You'd see it standing in the parlour like a small wooden church.
voor.Every day at noon, Walt: You'd hear the prices read out, slowly and clearly.
voor.In the Depression, nothing is wasted: You'd find a use for every scrap, every string and every nail.
voor.June has three dresses made from flour s: You'd never guess, looking at her, that they'd once held flour.
voor.Food is never wasted either: You'd see jars of beans and tomatoes lined up on the cellar shelves.
voor.The children make their own toys: You'd find a doll made from a corncob, or a top carved from a spool.
voor.In the Depression, America is full of tr: You'd see them walking along the road with a bundle on a stick.
voor.On the gatepost, at the end: You'd walk right past it, unless you knew what to look for.
voor.One day in the spring, a young man: You'd hear a soft knock at the kitchen door.
voor.In 1932 and 1933, many farmers: You can imagine how it felt to see your own farm on a sale poster.
voor.On the morning of the auction: You'd see dozens of trucks and wagons parked along the lane.
voor.June and Eddie go to a one-room school: You'd walk with them along the road, swinging your lunch pail.
voor.Inside the school, there is one big room: You'd smell chalk dust and wood smoke from the stove.
voor.The teacher is Miss Clara Holm: If you'd been her pupil, you'd have liked her, I'm sure.
voor.On Sunday morning, the Millers: You'd put on your best clothes and climb into the car.
voor.The neighbours help each other: You'd see five or six men working together in one field.
voor.One of the most popular programmes: You'd see young men in work clothes climbing into army trucks.
voor.The summer of 1933 comes to Iowa: You'd feel the heat rising off the dusty road.
voor.And at midday, there is the threshing di: You'd see long tables in the shade, piled high with food.
voor.On summer evenings, there is baseball: You'd hear the crack of the bat across the pasture.
voor.In the summer of 1933, there is a great: You'd hear people talking about it all over the county.
voor.In the evening, they stay to see the lig: You'd look up, and the whole sky would seem to glow.
voor.At the end of August, there is the count: You'd smell popcorn and hay the moment you walked through the gate.
voor.This year, Eddie is showing a calf: You'd see him brushing the calf until it shone.
voor.In October, the corn is ripe: You'd hear the dry leaves rustling as you walked down the rows.
voor.At the end of November, it is Thanksgivi: You'd smell pies cooling on the windowsill.
voor.In the late morning, the relatives arriv: You'd hear car doors slamming and voices calling hello.
voor.In December, the winter comes: You'd wake to frost patterns on the inside of the window.
voor.The children love the winter: You'd see them sliding down the hill behind the barn.
voor.The Great Depression did not end in 1933: You might think one good year would end it. It didn't.
voor.June went to college: You can picture her, a little nervous, stepping off the train.
voor.The people who lived through the Great D: You might know someone like that yourself, a grandparent perhaps.
voor.Today, Iowa is still farm country: If you drive there today, you'll still see cornfields to the horizon.
voor.Across Iowa, there are reminders: You could stop at an old stone shelter in a park and read the little sign.
voor.In some parts of Iowa, the old prairie: You'd walk through tall grass and wildflowers up to your waist.
